name: Spinocerebellar Ataxia

ethnicAssociations: SCA3 (Machado-Joseph disease) most common worldwide; particularly prevalent in Portuguese/Azorean, Brazilian, and Chinese populations
SCA1 relatively common in Italian, South African populations
SCA7 common in Scandinavian and South African populations

criteria.description: Progressive cerebellar ataxia (gait and/or limb ataxia)
Identification of pathogenic repeat expansion or mutation in a known SCA gene
Exclusion of acquired causes of cerebellar ataxia

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Progressive cerebellar ataxia with autosomal dominant family history or confirmed genetic mutation. Over 50 SCA types identified. Genetic testing is definitive.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Most common polyglutamine SCAs: SCA1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 17 (CAG repeat expansions). SCA3/MJD is most common worldwide. SCA6 is pure cerebellar and slowly progressive. SCA7 uniquely involves retinal degeneration. Anticipation (earlier onset in successive generations) common in polyglutamine SCAs.

pathognomonic.notes: Wide-based, unsteady gait; the defining feature of all SCAs
Intention tremor, finger-to-nose inaccuracy, heel-to-shin ataxia

common.notes: Gaze-evoked nystagmus, saccade abnormalities; slow saccades characteristic of SCA2
searchTerms: rapid eye jerks and abnormal eye control

common.notes: Difficulty with fine motor tasks, handwriting deterioration

searchTerms: pyramidal tract signs like muscle stiffness

occasional.notes: SCA2 and SCA3 can present with parkinsonism; SCA17 with chorea
searchTerms: movement disorders like stiffness and tremor
involuntary muscle contractions and slow movements

occasional.notes: More prominent in SCA17 and SCA2

rare.symptomName: Bulging eyes (lid retraction and external ophthalmoplegia)
searchTerms: bulging eyes with limited eye movement
wide-open eyes with eye muscle weakness

rare.notes: Lower motor neuron involvement in SCA3
searchTerms: involuntary muscle contractions with muscle loss

laboratory: Routine blood tests normal (used to exclude acquired causes)
Anti-GAD antibodies to exclude autoimmune cerebellar ataxia
Vitamin E, B12 levels to exclude nutritional causes
imaging: MRI brain: cerebellar atrophy (vermis and hemispheres)
Pontine atrophy (especially SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA7)
'Hot cross bun sign' in pons (SCA2, MSA-C differential)
Spinal cord atrophy in some subtypes
SCA6: relatively pure cerebellar atrophy without brainstem involvement
genetic: Over 50 SCA subtypes identified; many with known genes
other: Nerve conduction studies: axonal sensory neuropathy in some subtypes (SCA1, 2, 3)
Visual evoked potentials abnormal in SCA7
SARA (Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia) for disease monitoring

distinguishingFeatures: FA is autosomal recessive, not dominant
FA has areflexia and sensory neuropathy
MSA-C is sporadic without family history
MSA-C MRI shows hot cross bun sign and middle cerebellar peduncle changes
Has anti-GAD, anti-Yo, or other antibodies

redFlags: Rapidly progressive ataxia (weeks to months) suggests acquired cause (autoimmune, paraneoplastic, toxic) rather than SCA
Visual loss in ataxia patient should prompt SCA7 testing and ophthalmological evaluation
Anticipation (earlier onset in children) is characteristic of polyglutamine repeat disorders
Levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with ataxia may indicate SCA2 or SCA3
Absence of family history does not exclude SCA (de novo mutations, non-paternity, late onset in parent)
SCA6 can be episodic initially, mimicking episodic ataxia
references: Klockgether T, et al. Spinocerebellar ataxia. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2019;5(1):24.
Ashizawa T, et al. Spinocerebellar ataxias: prospects and challenges for therapy development. Nat Rev Neurol. 2018;14(10):590-605.
Durr A. Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias: polyglutamine expansions and beyond. Lancet Neurol. 2010;9(9):885-894.
commonPitfalls: Often misattributed to alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration due to overlapping gait and coordination symptoms.
Early psychiatric or cognitive symptoms may be overlooked, leading to misdiagnosis as primary psychiatric disorder.
Slow progression can be mistaken for non-progressive or static ataxias, such as congenital cerebellar hypoplasia.
Family history may be missed or underappreciated, especially with incomplete penetrance or de novo mutations.

extendedDiscriminators.feature: SCA typically presents with preserved tendon reflexes and normal cardiac function, whereas Friedreich ataxia often has absent lower limb reflexes and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
SCA usually lacks the prominent autonomic dysfunction (e.g., severe orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence) seen in MSA-C.
SCA has a gradual, progressive course and positive family history, while autoimmune cerebellar ataxia often has subacute onset and may respond to immunotherapy.

ruleOutCriteria: Absence of cerebellar atrophy on MRI in a patient with progressive ataxia and positive family history.
Demonstration of a pathogenic mutation in a gene not associated with SCA (e.g., FXN for Friedreich ataxia).
